name: Finding your way & weather
desc: Paper maps, compass, distance and time, no-phone navigation, clouds, weather signs, walking in the dark

s: Turn the map until it matches what you see: a road, river or coast on the map lines up with the real one (or use a compass).
Find where you are and keep your thumb on that spot as you walk.
Scale: on a 1:25,000 map, 4 cm is 1 km; on 1:50,000, 2 cm is 1 km.
Contour lines join points of the same height. Lines close together mean steep; far apart means flat.
The legend (key) explains the symbols: paths, woods, churches, water.
Tip: in the Netherlands and Italy you can still buy hiking and cycling maps; keep one in your bag.

guides.w: Find a direction and keep it
s: Hold the compass flat, away from metal, magnets and your phone. The red needle points north.
To head for a place on the map: lay the edge of the compass along the line from you to it, arrow pointing where you want to go.
Turn the dial until its lines run north–south on the map (N towards the top).
Lift the compass, hold it in front of you and turn your whole body until the red needle sits in the outline arrow (red in the shed).
Now the big arrow points your way. Pick a landmark in that direction, walk to it, and repeat.
In the Netherlands and Italy the difference between magnetic and map north is tiny: you can ignore it on foot.
Count your paces: count every time your left foot lands. Most adults do about 60–70 of these per 100 metres on flat ground. Test yours once.
Walking on the flat: about 4–5 km an hour.
Add about an hour for every 600 metres you climb (Naismith's rule).
Cycling: about 15 km an hour at an easy pace.
Things look closer than they are in clear air and over water, and further away in mist or at dusk.
Follow handrails: long, easy-to-follow things like a road, river, canal, railway or coastline.
Pick a catching feature beyond your goal (a road, a river) so you know if you've gone too far.
Aim off on purpose: head a bit to one side of a bridge or path, so when you hit the river or road you know which way to turn.
Look back often: the way home looks different from the other direction.
Ask people and look at signs: bus stops and churches often have the place name.
d: Don't push on when you're lost and it's getting dark: stop, think, and see the guide “Lost outdoors”

guides.w: What's coming in the next hours
s: High, thin wisps (mare's tails): often a change in the weather within a day.
Small, flat-bottomed fluffy clouds: fair weather.
Fluffy clouds that grow tall and dark during the day, with a flat top like an anvil: thunderstorm within hours. Get off hills and out of the water.
A low, grey blanket that thickens: steady rain on its way.
Wind suddenly turning cold and gusty: a storm or a shower is very close.
In the Netherlands, wind from the west or south-west usually brings rain from the sea.
A barometer falling fast (or a weather app that last showed falling pressure) means wind and rain coming.
Mountains and hills in summer: storms often build in the afternoon. Start early and be down by lunchtime.
Red sky in the evening often means a dry day tomorrow; a red sky in the morning can mean rain later.
A ring around the moon often comes before rain.

guides.w: When you didn't make it back before sunset
s: Give your eyes 20–30 minutes to get used to the dark. Bright light (even a phone screen) resets it.
Use a red or dim light if you can: it keeps your night vision.
At night you see better a little to the side of what you look at.
Walk slower, shorter steps, and keep to paths you can feel underfoot.
Stay together: agree to keep talking or within arm's length.
If the path gets dangerous (cliffs, water), stop and wait for light or help.
d: Don't take shortcuts in the dark
